# Deep learning in one chapter {#sec-ch05}

::: {.epigraph by="Arthur C. Clarke, Profiles of the Future, 1973"}
Any sufficiently advanced technology is indistinguishable from magic.
:::

"Deep learning" sounds like brain science mixed with magic. Good news: you've already met one. The logistic regression from Chapter 2 is a single artificial neuron. A deep network is many of them in layers, trained with the same downhill walk. Add a way to turn words into numbers and a way for words to look at each other, and you have the machinery inside every LLM. Four ideas, each simpler than it sounds.

::: {.goals}
- See why one neuron can only draw a straight line, and how layers and a simple "hinge" let a network draw almost any shape.
- Explain how an embedding turns words into points where closeness means similar meaning.
- Describe attention as each word asking which other words matter to it.
- Explain why big models trained for long tend to become overconfident, and how to fix it.
:::

## Idea one: layers bend the line

A neuron multiplies each clue by a weight, adds them up and squashes the total into a probability. That means it can only cut the world in two with a straight edge. But some behaviour is suspicious when it's *unusual in any direction*: far too much activity or far too little, far too early or too late. No straight line separates the middle from the edges.

![A toy problem. Blue dots are normal activity; red crosses surround them on every side. One neuron (left) can only draw a straight line through it. With a hidden layer of three neurons (middle) the boundary becomes a triangle; with twelve (right), close to a circle.](/figures/ch06/line-limit.pdf){#fig-line-limit}

The fix is to send the clues to a few neurons first. Each one draws its own line, and an output neuron combines *their* answers. Three straight edges make a triangle. Twelve make something close to a circle (@fig-line-limit), and the log loss drops from {{< num ch06 toy_lr f2 >}} to {{< num ch06 toy_net12 f2 >}}. The layers in between are **hidden**, and a network with several of them is **deep**. That's all "deep" means.

One detail makes it work. A sum of sums is still a sum, so each hidden neuron *bends* its answer first: negative becomes zero, positive passes through. This **ReLU** is a hinge, and enough hinges can draw almost any curve. *Weighted sums draw lines; hinges bend them; layers combine the bends.*

Training is the same downhill walk. The only new problem is finding the slope for a weight several layers deep, and the answer, **backpropagation**, is easiest to picture as sharing out blame: the error at the output is passed back, layer by layer, to each weight in proportion to its part in it [@rumelhart1986].

Why depth matters: on photos, early layers learn edges, later ones textures and shapes, the last ones whole objects [@lecun2015]. Nobody wrote a rule for "edge". A deep network takes raw input and *learns its own clues*.

On neat, hand-made features there's nothing left for it to find. A small network does as well as logistic regression, but no better: log loss {{< num ch06 k_small.log_loss f3 >}} against {{< num ch06 k_lr.log_loss f3 >}}. A big one trained too long gets worse: {{< num ch06 k_big.log_loss f3 >}}.

::: {.keyidea}
Deep networks are worth their cost on raw, messy input. On neat features, start with something simple.
:::

## Idea two: meaning as geometry

A network does arithmetic, so words must become numbers. Number them in a list ("invoice" 101, "bill" 102, "lunch" 103) and the maths decides "bill" is halfway between "invoice" and "lunch". Nonsense. Neither numbering knows anything about meaning.

The fix came from linguistics: *you know a word by the company it keeps*. "phishing" and "spoofed" rarely share a sentence, but they turn up in the same *kinds* of places, near "email" and "password". Count which words appear near each word, squash the counts into a short list of numbers, and words used alike get similar lists. That list is an **embedding**.

![Word vectors learned from 30,000 synthetic analyst notes, with similar vectors placed close together. Each card is a family of words the method discovered on its own, from context alone: kinds of lure, kinds of malware, kinds of secret.](/figures/ch07/word-map.pdf){#fig-word-map}

Nobody told it that "trojan", "ransomware" and "backdoor" belong together; it found out from context alone (@fig-word-map). Closeness is measured by the angle between two vectors, **cosine similarity**: about 1 for the same direction, about 0 for unrelated.

The same trick works for whole documents: similar alerts land near each other, so you can ask "show me past cases like this one". It's the engine inside RAG (Chapter 7). But test it: for each alert, find its 50 most similar past alerts by text, and count how many were attacks. That gives a calibrated probability, with a calibration error of {{< num ch07 knn.ece f3 >}}. But it ranks alerts poorly: its AUC is {{< num ch07 knn.auc f2 >}}, against {{< num ch07 lr.auc f2 >}} for logistic regression on the fields. To an embedding, two "large upload" alerts look the same whether the threat score is 0.05 or 0.95.

::: {.keyidea}
Embeddings capture what things are about. They're poor at the exact numbers inside them.
:::

## Idea three: words that look at each other

One vector per word isn't enough. "invoice, not phishing" clears an alert; "phishing, not invoice" raises one. Same three words. A model that only knows *which words appear* sees two identical notes.

**Attention** fixes this, and fits in one sentence: *every word asks which other words should change its meaning, and listens to them in proportion.*

![The word "phishing" asks a question (the query), compares it with each word's label (key), turns the matches into weights that sum to 1, and takes that mix of their contents (values). In the trained model, it looks almost entirely at "not".](/figures/ch08/qkv.pdf){#fig-qkv}

Each word makes a **query** ("what am I looking for?"), a **key** ("what can I tell you about?") and a **value** (what it passes on). Compare every query with every key, turn the scores into weights that add up to 1 (a **softmax**), and take the weighted mix of the values (@fig-qkv). That's the Q, K and V in every attention diagram.

Train one attention layer on 4,000 tiny notes where "not" flips the meaning. A model that only counts words (a "bag of words") reaches {{< num ch08 acc_bow pct >}} accuracy at best. Attention reaches {{< num ch08 acc_att pct >}}. Look inside, and you can see what it learned.

![What each word attends to after training. In "invoice not phishing", the word "phishing" puts nearly all its attention on "not". Nobody told the model about negation; it found that looking at the word before was the cheapest way to get the answers right.](/figures/ch08/heatmaps.pdf){#fig-heatmaps}

"phishing" puts {{< num ch08 att_phishing_to_not pct >}} of its attention on "not" (@fig-heatmaps).

A **transformer** is attention plus a small network on each word, stacked dozens of times [@vaswani2017]. It won because attention looks at every pair of words *at once*, which runs in parallel on graphics chips. One distinction matters for this book. A **reader** (encoder) lets every word see the whole input: right for understanding and deciding. A **writer** (decoder) lets each word see only earlier words: necessary for writing, since word six doesn't exist while you write word five. LLMs are writers.

::: {.keyidea}
Readers see everything at once and suit deciding; writers see only the past and suit writing. LLMs are writers.
:::

## Idea four: scale, and a side effect

How did stacked attention learn to write essays? Mostly by getting bigger, on a task that needs no labels: hide the next word of any text, and guess it. Every sentence ever written becomes free training data, and guessing well forces the model to learn grammar, facts and a surprising amount of reasoning. This **pretraining** improves smoothly and predictably with size, data and computing power [@kaplan2020].

Two more stages make an assistant: **instruction tuning** on examples of good answers, then **preference tuning** on which answers people prefer [@ouyang2022]. People prefer answers that sound sure. OpenAI's own GPT-4 report showed the pretrained model's confidence was well calibrated, and clearly less so after preference tuning [@openai2023].

You can watch a deeper version of this on our alerts. Train a network far bigger than the job needs, for a long time, and check it on test alerts.

![The same training run, on test alerts. Accuracy (left) barely moves. Log loss (middle) and calibration error (right) are flat for a while, then climb steeply. Watch only accuracy and you'd never notice.](/figures/ch09/overtraining.pdf){#fig-overtraining}

Accuracy barely changed. Meanwhile, the test log loss went from {{< num ch09 first.log_loss f2 >}} to {{< num ch09 last.log_loss f2 >}}, and the calibration error went from {{< num ch09 first.ece f3 >}} to {{< num ch09 last.ece f3 >}} (@fig-overtraining). The model still *ranked* alerts well. But it was no longer *calibrated*.

Why? Once a model gets most training examples right, the only way left to lower log loss is to push correct answers towards certainty: 0.95, 0.99, 0.999. A flexible model trained long enough becomes certain of everything it saw, noise included, and carries that certainty to new cases where it isn't earned [@guo2017].

::: {.keyidea}
Flexible models trained to make their training loss as small as possible learn to be too certain.
:::

The fixes are the ones you know. Stop training when held-out loss stops improving (here, around pass {{< num ch09 best_epoch int >}} through the data). Then recalibrate on unseen data: one temperature cut the calibration error from {{< num ch09 last.ece f3 >}} to {{< num ch09 ece_after_T f3 >}}. A correction makes the numbers honest again; it can't give back what memorising lost.

::: {.breaks}
Networks need lots of data, and with too little they memorise. They're hard to read: there's no tidy "×2.9 for a new country". Embeddings copy the associations in their training text, including stereotypes [@bolukbasi2016]. They're also bad at negation, since "malicious" and "not malicious" appear next to almost the same words. It's tempting to read attention maps as explanations, but in large models they often aren't [@jain2019]. And you usually can't retrain someone else's big model, or even see its raw probabilities. That's one reason it matters so much to have a decision model that returns probabilities as its main output, and to test them.
:::

::: {.threshold}
Your team replaces the logistic regression with a big network because its training loss is lower. They keep the same threshold: alerts below P = 0.03 close automatically. Will more or fewer real threats be closed without a person seeing them?

(More. The big network is overconfident: many alerts it pushes near zero aren't really that safe. The threshold assumed calibrated probabilities. Recalibrate first and check the threshold again, or keep the simpler model.)
:::

::: {.exercises}
1. Why does a network with no hinges collapse to a single straight line, however many layers it has?
2. In your own words, and without the letters Q, K or V, explain what attention does for "phishing" in "invoice not phishing".
3. A vendor's classifier is "97% accurate" and returns a confidence with every prediction. You plan to act automatically above 0.9. What would you ask for before agreeing?
:::

::: {.nexthook}
Next: what does an LLM actually do when it writes? It writes one token at a time, with a probability for every possible next piece. That detail matters a great deal for decisions.
:::
